Let $S=k+m+n$. Observe that every term on the right–hand side of the recurrence also has coordinate sum $S$, so the problem decouples into independent systems for each fixed even $S\ge 0$.

Write $k=2a,\;m=2b,\;n=2c$ with $a,b,c\in\mathbb Z_{\ge0}$, set $N=a+b+c=S/2$, and define $f(a,b,c)=T(2a,2b,2c)$.  
The boundary condition $kmn=0$ becomes $abc=0$, giving $f=2N$ on the boundary. For $a,b,c>0$:
$$f(a,b,c)=3+\frac16\sum_{\text{6 neighbours}} f(\text{neighbour}),$$
where the neighbours are obtained by transferring one unit between coordinates (e.g. $(a+1,b-1,c)$, etc.).

This is the standard mean–value equation for a random walk on the discrete triangle $a+b+c=N$ that accumulates cost $3$ per step until it hits the boundary. Hence
$$f(a,b,c)=3\,\mathbb E[\tau]+\text{boundary payoff}=3\,\mathbb E[\tau]+2N.$$

To find $\mathbb E[\tau]$, note that for $g(a,b,c)=abc$ a direct computation gives the average over the six neighbours:
$$\frac16\sum g(\text{neighbour})=abc-\frac{a+b+c}{3}=abc-\frac N3.$$
Thus $Lg:=\frac16\sum g-g=-\frac N3$, so the function $h(a,b,c)=\frac{9abc}{N}$ satisfies $Lh=-3$ in the interior. Adding the harmonic function $2N$ (which equals $2N$ on the boundary) gives a solution:
$$f(a,b,c)=2N+\frac{9abc}{a+b+c}.$$

By the maximum principle on the finite state space, this solution is unique for each $N$. Returning to $k,m,n$ (so $a=k/2$, etc., and $N=S/2$):
$$T(k,m,n)=S+\frac{9\cdot\frac k2\cdot\frac m2\cdot\frac n2}{S/2}
= k+m+n+\frac{9kmn}{4(k+m+n)}.$$

When $k+m+n>0$ and some coordinate is $0$, the fraction vanishes and $T=k+m+n$, agreeing with the given boundary condition. The remaining point $(0,0,0)$ is prescribed to be $0$.

Thus there is exactly one such function:

$$\boxed{T(k,m,n)=k+m+n+\dfrac{9kmn}{4(k+m+n)}\quad\text{for }k+m+n>0,\ \text{and }T(0,0,0)=0}$$

(equivalently $T(2a,2b,2c)=2(a+b+c)+\dfrac{9abc}{a+b+c}$ for nonnegative integers $a,b,c$ not all zero).
